item.title: The Quiet Thing Loneliness Does to Your Memory
item.description:
Loneliness

The Quiet Thing Loneliness Does to Your Memory

Loneliness doesn’t make you remember bad moments more. It makes good ones disappear.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • Lonely people recall fewer positive social memories, not more negative ones.
  • The brain in lonely mode doesn’t add darkness. It subtracts light.
  • This memory gap helps explain why loneliness tends to become chronic.
  • Actively recalling positive moments can help interrupt the loop.
Some moments stay. Others leave quietly, and we don't notice they're gone.
Source: Samuel Austin / Unsplash

The standard picture of a lonely brain goes something like this: hypervigilant, threat-scanning, reading hostility into neutral faces, flinching at ambiguous texts. And that picture isn't wrong; research on social threat sensitivity in loneliness is well-established.

But it misses something. It focuses on what loneliness adds to perception, and overlooks what it removes.

What a 2024 Study Found About Loneliness and Memory Bias

A large-scale study published in the British Journal of Social Psychology asked a straightforward question: Do chronically lonely people show a negative bias in how they remember social experiences (Igarashi, 2024)?

The researchers analysed autobiographical memories from over 4,000 participants across four separate datasets. Participants were asked to recall a recent social episode, either positive, negative, or neutral.

The results were not what most people would predict. Lonely individuals were no more likely than others to recall negative social experiences. Both groups were similarly inclined to remember the bad moments.

Where the groups differed was on positive memeories: Lonely individuals recalled significantly fewer positive social experiences than their less lonely counterparts.

The problem wasn't that the darkness had intensified. It was that the light had gone quiet.

Why Recalling Positive Social Experiences Matters More Than You Might Think

This distinction isn't just semantic; it changes how you understand the loop.

If loneliness were simply about seeing threats everywhere, the solution would be to challenge those perceptions head-on, to interrogate the distortion. But if the real mechanism is the fading of positive memories, the distortion is harder to catch. There is nothing obviously wrong with your perception of any given moment. The warmth and kindness of your friend texting you and staying late was there. It just doesn't get filed—or when it does, it doesn't stay.

Researcher John Cacioppo, who spent decades mapping the neuroscience of loneliness, described the phenomenon as a feedback loop: Loneliness shifts how the brain processes social information, those shifts make genuine connection harder to register, and the resulting lack of registered connection deepens the loneliness (Cacioppo & Patrick, 2008). What this newer research adds is a specific mechanism for part of that loop. The positive experiences aren't necessarily absent; they're just not making it into the archive.

The Practical Problem

I think about a specific kind of conversation that happens inside this loop, the internal one: When you feel lonely for long enough, you start to take inventory. Does anyone actually reach out first? Do people remember what I've told them? Is this friendship mutual? The audit feels rational. What it doesn't account for is that the data you're auditing is incomplete. The positive evidence has been systematically underweighted because a lonely brain doesn't encode it the same way.

This is how loneliness becomes self-sustaining without feeling like a distortion. It feels like an accurate reading of the evidence. And in a sense, it is, just not of the complete evidence.

What This Points Toward

The research doesn't offer a clean fix, and I'd be skeptical of any that claimed to. But it does suggest something specific worth trying: If positive social memories are the thing that's going missing, deliberately recalling them is not sentimental self-help. It is, in a fairly literal sense, correcting an incomplete record.

You don't need to generate a list of reasons to feel better. You instead can try to access specific memories, with specific people, recalled in enough detail that the brain can process them as social evidence rather than abstract reassurance. The friend who drove 40 minutes to help you move or the message that arrived exactly when you needed it. The small, unremarkable afternoon that, if you stop and think about it, was not unremarkable at all.

The loneliness didn't erase those moments. It just didn't keep them somewhere easy to find.

item.title: What Should Parents Know About Their Teen’s Troubles?
item.description:
Law and Crime

What Should Parents Know About Their Teen’s Troubles?

With greater potential for liability, parents must learn what to look for.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • In some cases of teenage violence, parents have been held liable for related charges.
  • Parents can learn from research about red flag behaviors for potential future violence in kids.
  • With education comes protection for all parties.
Source: Art by K. Ramsland

At the end of May, a teenage girl allegedly stabbed three horses stabled at a barrel racing competition in Las Vegas. Caught on video, she was arrested. A judge decided she posed a danger to the public, so she remained in detention. She faces charges for willful or malicious killing, maiming or torturing an animal, and felony malicious destruction of property.

On social media, there was an immediate call for charging the girl’s parents as well. Some people acquainted with the suspect’s past behavior said there’d been signs of trouble.

What this girl allegedly did justifies outrage, but we need more clarity about when to hold parents accountable. Over the past few years, we’ve seen some cases in which parents have been convicted of negligence (and worse) when they ignored their child’s troubling behavioral signals.

In Michigan in 2021, Oxford High School officials told James and Jennifer Crumbley that their fifteen-year-old son, Ethan, appeared to be in crisis. They were asked to remove him from school. They refused. That day, he used a handgun to kill four students and injure six others and a teacher. The parents were both convicted of involuntary manslaughter and sentenced to 10-15 years. It was the first time that parents had been held criminally responsible for their child’s mass school shooting.

The argument was that Ethan’s behavior presented red flags that his parents had ignored: He’d told his mother he’d seen demons, he’d drawn disturbing images at school that they knew about, and he’d been researching ammunition. Just three days before the attack, Jennifer had taken him to a shooting range with a 9-millimeter handgun his father had purchased for him.

More recently, Colin Gray, the father of the fourteen-year-old Apalachee High School shooter Colt Gray, was found guilty in March of second-degree murder, involuntary manslaughter, reckless conduct, and cruelty to children. Colt had carried out a mass shooting on September 4, 2024, killing two students and two teachers, and wounding nine others. Colin Gray was found to be responsible for ignoring warnings that his son was a potential danger to others. Instead, he’d purchased the AR-15-style rifle that his son had used, had left his own weapons unsecured, and had allowed the boy easy access to ammunition.

Prosecutor Patricia Brooks used testimony from Colt’s relatives who’d seen his deteriorating mental health to show that Gray had foreknowledge and requests for restricting firearms. The boy even had a photo of the Parkland school shooter, Nikolas Cruz, on his bedroom wall. In addition, law enforcement had warned Gray about an FBI tip that his son was involved in an online threat to shoot up the school. In his defense, Gray claimed, “There was this whole other side of Colt I didn’t know existed.” The jury didn’t buy it.

Although risk evaluation for future violence isn’t easy, even for professionals, sometimes a parental lapse seems clear. When others pay the price, they want accountability. Even if parents of violent kids fail to understand the signs, juries consider whether they’ve ignored warnings from those who do.

No one can be aware of or control their kids 24/7, but criminal responsibility emphasizes evidence of neglect or a failure to act when behavioral signs of violence are present.

The parents of Tycen Proper, 19, noticed something wrong. He’d just finished high school but seemed uninterested in pursuing an occupation. His mother saw him studying maps of Washington, D.C., and noted a more intense interest in religion. He’d used his graduation money to buy a rifle, a shotgun, body armor, and ammunition. He also distanced himself from his parents. The Propers contacted authorities.

An investigation showed that Tycen and a small group of co-conspirators were preparing to assassinate President Donald Trump and others at the UFC event held at the White House on June 14. They allegedly believed their attack would trigger a revolution. Parental awareness and action blocked them before they could pull this off.

According to the Columbia University Irving Medical Center site, risk factors for future violence in kids include the following: exposure to violence at home, being bullied, parental neglect, substance abuse, fascination with weapons or violent individuals, feeling rejected, and poor school performance. This website offers examples of behavior to watch for, and several plans of action should parents be concerned.

Harvard Pilgrim Healthcare also offers such tips: “There can be many signs that children or teens may be thinking about being violent. For example, they may get into fights. They may bully others, hurt animals, or damage someone's property. Other signs include talking or posting on social media about violence and withdrawing from friends, family, and activities.” They include a list of steps to take to be proactive.

Prison psychologist Al Carlisle collected a list of traits in adolescent boys common to those who’d likely to commit sexual or fatal assaults. They were typically socially awkward, the butt of jokes, had low self-esteem, poor performance in school, a persistent sense of failure, domineering females in their lives, early involvement with antisocial activities, experiences of rejection, a heavy dependence on others, and a tendency to fluctuate between emotional inhibition and flashes of anger.

Dr. Peter Langman, a clinical psychologist and an expert on school shooters, published Warning Signs: Identifying School Shooters before They Strike. He has built a comprehensive website, www.schoolshooters.info, to keep track of such incidents.

“There is no one cause of school shootings,” he says, “there is no one intervention that will prevent school shootings, and there is no one profile of a school shooter.” However, there are some distinct behaviors that can alert us to a potential shooter. Rage and frustration are prominent. Prior to acting, they might brag, warn, threaten, praise other shooters, join a movement, try to recruit others to a cause, and display a “nothing to lose” mentality.

“School shootings are the culmination of a long process,” Langman states. “When the attacker has determined time, place, and method and has obtained the necessary means, time is precious.” The more specific a plan is, the more likely it is to be carried out.

In light of increased pressure to make parents share responsibility for what their kids do, parents should become informed about common red-flag behaviors and prepare themselves with resources for intervention. Even if they fail to stop a violent act, they can show the efforts they made. The legal cases against parents who ignored their child’s troubled behavior offer cautionary tales.

item.title: How 5 Classic Rom-Coms Teach Us to Love Better
item.description:
Relationships

How 5 Classic Rom-Coms Teach Us to Love Better

Before swiping, we learned about love from the movies we watched together.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • A 2013 study found that watching rom-coms to learn about love was linked to stronger romantic beliefs.
  • Millennials and Gen Z have come of age with fewer rom-coms modeling real relationship dynamics.
  • Rom-coms from 1961 to 2004 offer concrete lessons on vulnerability, risk-taking, and daily commitment.

Social media has somewhat altered how we view romantic love, and some studies show it has increased relationship dissatisfaction and disconnection. For instance, 51% of couples feel their partner is easily distracted by their cellphones when they are trying to talk to them; 40% feel annoyed by how much time their partners spend on their phones; and 34% go through their partner’s phone without asking.

Just among millennials, social media appears to have increased conflict—and infidelity rates. In fact, therapists are seeing an increased number of couples with heightened relational distress due to social media, such as flirting with someone online and engaging in emotionally inappropriate chats with other people. Another possible factor: With a decline in the number of romantic comedies (rom-coms) produced over the last decade, millennials and Generation Z may not get to experience them in the way many Gen Xers and Boomers did, i.e., as potential learning experiences about dating and navigating relationships.

A 2013 peer-reviewed psychological study surveyed undergraduates and found that those who watch rom-coms with the intention of learning about relationships tend to hold stronger romantic beliefs than those who watch for other reasons, such as entertainment or boredom. Mood can enhance sociability, suggesting that if romantic comedies can positively influence mood, then viewing these movies may be a particularly useful societal activity. When positive emotions are generated through media exposure, they can help reduce stress and create many beneficial feelings.

Following are 5 rom-coms from 1960 to 2004 that could teach us a thing or two about dating and love—and they may add a little joy to one’s life.

Breakfast at Tiffany's
Source: Paramount Pictures

Breakfast at Tiffany’s (1961): A young New York socialite (Audrey Hepburn) becomes interested in a handsome young man (George Peppard) who has moved into her apartment building, but her highly avoidant attachment style gets in the way. She even refuses to name her own cat, so that she and the cat will not become too attached. Just imagine how she feels about relationships with humans. What we can learn: love requires vulnerability.

What's Up Doc?
Source: Warner Bros.

What’s Up, Doc? (1972): Two researchers (Barbara Streisand and Ryan O’Neal) have come to San Francisco to compete for a research grant in music. Judy pursues Howard romantically, and in the process, disrupts his rigid lifestyle. What we can learn about love: Sometimes following the checklist to find a partner does not work. Sometimes you must act on unplanned, spontaneous romantic chemistry.

Tootsie
Source: Columbia Pictures

Tootsie (1982): Michael Dorsey (Dustin Hoffman) is a talented out-of-work actor in New York City who reinvents himself as an actress to get hired by a soap opera and then falls for one of the show's leading ladies (Jessica Lange). Because Michael lives as a woman for work, he develops greater empathy for women and eventually becomes a better romantic partner. What we learn about love: Through understanding the lived experience of someone we love, we can form a deeper connection.

Sleepless in Seattle
Source: Sony Pictures Entertainment

Sleepless in Seattle (1993): After his wife's death, Sam Baldwin (Tom Hanks) moves to Seattle with his son. His son calls in to a talk-radio program hoping to find a new wife for his father, eventually leading to his father meeting Annie Reed (Meg Ryan). What we can learn about love: imagining a love, taking a risk, and following one’s heart is the harder option, but one with the better payoff than the safe-but-uninspired one, such as Annie’s relationship with her fiancé, Walter.

50 First Dates
Source: Columbia Pictures

50 First Dates (2004): Playboy veterinarian Henry (Adam Sandler) sets his sights on romancing Lucy (Drew Barrymore), but she suffers from short-term memory loss; she can’t remember anything that happened the day before. What we can learn about love: love is not a one-time declaration, but a daily, continuous effort, and romantic commitment is an active choice.

item.title: Dreams and Dreamers in "The Odyssey"
item.description:
Dreaming

Dreams and Dreamers in "The Odyssey"

"The Odyssey" warns against seeing in dreams what we want to see.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • Homer’s poems portray dreams as difficult to understand and potentially deceptive.
  • Dreams are also shown as bringing reassurance and guidance in times of uncertainty.
  • The Odyssean fallacy is the tendency to read one’s own desires into someone else’s dream.
Source: Kelly Bulkeley

Among the many gifts of Homer’s two epic poems are vital insights into the nature and meaning of dreams, insights that are still relevant today. The story of The Odyssey was preceded by The Iliad, whose dream references provide a helpful context for the later tale.

In just the second book of The Iliad, a god-sent dream plays a pivotal role. However, in this case, the dream is a cruel deception sent by Zeus to the Greek leader Agamemnon, encouraging him to launch an attack he is destined to lose. This incident in The Iliad, one of the most influential works of all antiquity, shows that people of this time were aware of the danger of believing too easily in the pleasing fantasies of dreams.

Women Dreamers

The dreams reported in The Odyssey all come from women, and they all have multiple dimensions of meaning. The first comes to Queen Penelope, the wife of Odysseus, who falls into despair when she realizes her son Telemachus has secretly left home to seek his long-lost father. That night the goddess Athena sends Penelope a dream in the trustworthy form of her sister to deliver a message of comfort and reassurance. When Penelope awakens, she feels remarkably better, “her spirit warmed now that a dream so clear had come to her in darkest night.” This is a slightly deceptive dream, in that an external agent deliberately shapes a familiar dream image to elicit a specific emotional reaction from the dreamer. The result is clearly favorable for the dreamer, and yet the story also provides the audience with a higher critical awareness of the subtle dynamics of external (divine) influences on the dreaming process.

Athena is also behind the next dream reference. She sends a dream to Nausicaa, a young princess, using the form of Nausicaa’s best friend who urges the princess to go to the river to wash her finest clothing in readiness for her wedding day. When Nausicaa awakens, “still beguiled by her dream,” she goes with her laundry to the river, and there she suddenly encounters a wild, magnificent, naked man—Odysseus himself. The great warrior is lost and alone, and so Athena has helpfully sent a dream that puts the king’s daughter in an amorous mood and guides her to where she, and only she, will find Odysseus and personally escort him back to the safety of the royal palace.

This is a dream that in its primary purpose is intended by Athena to serve the needs of Odysseus, not Nausicaa. Athena is using Nausicaa as a means of enabling Odysseus to continue his journey home. And yet, the dream does not harm or mislead the dreamer. It may even help her in prompting a greater degree of self-awareness of her latent romantic desires. The goddess, the warrior, and the princess all benefit from this dream in different ways.

The Odyssean Fallacy

The most dramatic dream scene in The Odyssey occurs near the end, when Odysseus finally returns home after 20 years but does not yet reveal himself to his wife Penelope. Disguised as a beggar, he meets with Penelope to gain information about the brutish men, the “suitors” (108 of them), who have invaded his palace to press their affections on the apparently widowed Penelope. During this meeting, the queen shares a dream with the beggar. “Listen closely,” she says. In the dream, she tends her 20 geese—“I love to watch them all”—when suddenly a mountain eagle swoops down and kills all the geese, then flies away again. Then a voice in the dream says that the geese are the suitors and Odysseus the eagle, about to return and kill them all.

When Penelope finishes, the beggar/Odysseus instantly replies, “Dear woman, twist it however you like, your dream can only mean one thing”: death to the suitors. But Penelope says, “Ah my friend, dreams are hard to unravel,” and she goes on to give a remarkable speech about the two gates of dreams, one of ivory for false dreams and one of polished horn for dreams “fraught with truth, for the dreamer who can see them.”

The meaning of Penelope’s dream and her two gates speech depends on what we think is happening between these two people. If we accept that Odysseus has successfully disguised his identity from Penelope, then we are likely to accept his interpretation, wonder at her puzzling resistance, and regard the subsequent slaughter of the suitors as validating his reading of her dream.

However, if we remember that Penelope has proven herself to be the most savvy and intelligent of women, a different possibility emerges. She does know who the beggar really is, and she poses her dream to him as a riddle. The 20 geese in her dream, in this view, symbolize not the 108 suitors, but the 20 years that Odysseus has been gone from her and their family, fighting in someone else’s war. He has killed those 20 years of their life together—does he see that? Does he see her?

Sadly, no. He sees what he wants to see, in what I call the Odyssean fallacy of dream interpretation. He offers a self-validating analysis of her dream that ignores her lived reality and foregrounds his own selfish desires. Penelope’s two gates speech, in this reading, is a subtle but unmistakable way of saying he has failed her test. Immediately after this, she announces the contest of the bow and axes. He could have won her right then if he had properly understood her dream; now, alas, he must prove himself in another, much more dangerous way.

Not all retellings of The Odyssey include these dream scenes. But the oneiric wisdom in these passages from Homer’s ancient epics continues to shape and inspire the way we think about dreams today.

item.title: Beyond the Therapy Room: Why Lived Experience Matters
item.description:
Therapy

Beyond the Therapy Room: Why Lived Experience Matters

Much of the therapeutic journey happens when the therapist is not there.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • Much of the work of therapy happens between appointments, not during them
  • People with lived experience may help clients make sense of therapy in ways professionals alone sometimes cant
  • As psychotherapy evolves, we should see peer mentors not as optional but integral to good psychological care

by Michael Mo

I have always found it interesting that we tend to talk about psychotherapy as though it only exists inside the therapy room, especially when we talk about it with our colleagues.

A client attends for 50 minutes, we formulate, explore, challenge, reflect, and agree on homework and then they leave until next week. This is how therapists usually speak about their work in professional and sometimes personal settings.

My experience is teaching me something rather different.

Can Sharing Lived Experience Help Clients Make Sense of Therapy?

Some of the most important therapeutic moments happen after the session has finished. They happen when someone is walking home replaying the conversation in their head. They happen when they try something different with their partner or notice an old pattern creeping back. They happen while sitting in a café wondering whether what the therapist said actually makes sense in real life.

We all speak about the importance of homework with clients to extend their therapy journey between sessions. But deep down, we know that the number of clients who complete their homework is smaller than the number who do. So, in my experience, the client’s own reflections and exploration to change are less effectively utilised.

We all know that the consulting room is where therapy begins. Life is where it is tested.

Then how do we make the best of the time outside therapy appointments?

This idea has become something of a personal passion for me, particularly since introducing peer mentors into the service in which I work.

A peer mentor is someone who has travelled a similar therapeutic journey themselves. They are not therapists and they are certainly not there to replace therapy. Instead, they walk alongside people who are just beginning that journey, offering something that textbooks simply cannot provide: genuine lived experience.

Working predominantly with military veterans has probably strengthened my belief in this more than anything else.

Military culture places enormous value on experience. It is not unusual to hear veterans ask: “Has this person actually done it?” They are not questioning professional qualifications. They are trying to understand whether the other person truly appreciates what the journey feels like.

There is a quiet credibility that comes from someone saying, “I’ve sat in that chair too.”

Interestingly, I think psychotherapy has something to learn from that.

What Can Peer Mentors Teach Therapists?

One of the reasons I enjoy practising Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is because it gives people practical ways of understanding themselves. The models are elegant, the research is extensive and the evidence is strong. But knowing a model and living through it are not always the same thing.

Learning CBT reminds me of learning almost anything else.

You can attend lessons every week, listen carefully and understand all the theory. But real learning happens afterwards. It happens when you try something, get it wrong, talk to your friends about it, think about it differently and then come back ready to learn some more.

Therapy follows the same pattern.

When our peer mentors meet clients for a coffee, they are not delivering another therapy session. Quite the opposite. They are helping people digest therapy. Clients often talk through ideas they have struggled to process in the consulting room. Sometimes they realise what an intervention actually meant only after explaining it aloud to someone else. Sometimes they simply need reassurance that feeling uncertain is part of the process.

Those conversations might not appear in any treatment manual, yet I suspect they are doing far more therapeutic work than we often recognise.

There is also something wonderfully human about lived experience.

The Growing Research on the Benefits of Peer Mentors

As therapists, we inevitably bring professional knowledge into the room. That is our role. We formulate, guide, challenge and maintain safe boundaries. Peer mentors bring something different. They offer hope in its most practical form. They demonstrate that recovery is not simply a concept discussed in supervision or described in research papers; it is something another person has actually lived.

The growing evidence around peer support in mental health is encouraging (Aitken & Kinane, 2024, Ranzenhofer, et al, 2020, Francia et al, 2023), suggesting improvements in engagement, hope and recovery when lived-experience roles complement clinical care. I suspect research will continue to strengthen over the coming years. But even before we look at the data, many of us have already seen its impact sitting quietly in front of us. Sometimes the things that matter most in healthcare are recognised in practice before they are fully explained by research.

Perhaps this reflects a wider change in how we think about psychological therapy.

For many years we have worked hard to establish psychotherapy as a rigorous, evidence-based profession. That has been enormously important, and rightly so. But somewhere along the way, I wonder whether we have occasionally given the impression that therapy is something professionals do to people.

Increasingly I see it as something built together.

The therapist brings knowledge of psychology. The client brings knowledge of themselves. The peer mentor brings knowledge of the journey. None of these forms of expertise replace one another; together they create something richer than any of them could provide alone.

For me, peer mentoring is not about replacing therapy with lived experience. It is about recognising that psychological change rarely happens because of a single conversation each week. It happens through hundreds of small moments of reflection, practice, doubt, encouragement and discovery.

Our profession has spent many years perfecting what happens once the client enters the therapy room.

Perhaps the next step for us is to recognise, value and nurture everything that happens once the client walks back out.

Michael Mo
Source: Michael Mo

Michael Mo is Clinical Lead for Veterans NHS Wales at Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board. He is a BABCP-accredited Cognitive Behavioural Therapist as well as an ISST Advanced Certified Individual Schema Therapist and Supervisor. His main focus is complex trauma and personality difficulties, including elements of addiction and neurodiversity.
